column2: The consolidation of the Griffon states under Grover the first and his successors revolutionized military strategy. With the advent of cheap small arms and the rise of the drafted citizen soldiers, armies grew rapidly in size to become massed formations. This necessitated dividing the army first into divisions and later into corps. Along with divisions came divisional artillery.

Barbed Wire was a late tenth-century Equestrian invention, used originally to protect southern settlements from Buffalo raiders. Barbed Wire became integrated with the trench systems of the Great War as it was relatively easy to string up and often survived artillery bombardments and machine gun fire. The sharp barbs caused injury to attacking infantry. Emplacing rows of barbed wire in front of the trench line gave the machine gunners and field batteries time to decimate an attack while it was stuck cutting the wire.

For centuries bladed weapons had been the frontline weapon of choice for armies. Originally created by local blacksmiths, the advent of professional armies and mass conscription necessitated mass production of standardized weapons. Although long superseded by modern firearms, bladed weapons enjoy continuing popularity as ceremonial weapons for parades and demonstrations.
The Gaitling gun, patented in 961 by Grape Shot, was the first to offer controlled, sequential fire with automatic loading. It first saw very limited action in the Buffalo Frontier Wars.

Bolt action is a type of firearm action in which the weapon's bolt is operated manually by the opening and closing of the breech (barrel) with a small handle. The first bolt-action rifle was produced in 824 by Johann Niclaws von Dreyse, following work on breechloading rifles. Equestrian and Griffonian armies continued to develop bolt-action rifles through the latter half of the Tenth Century and The Great War marked the height of the bolt-action rifle's use, with all of the nations in that war fielding troops armed with various bolt-action designs.

Quick-Firing Field Guns are breech-loaded artillery pieces that combine several characteristics to produce a high rate of fire. Buffer mechanisms and self-contained ammunition limited and then eliminated recoil of the barrel. Innovations in breech technology allowed for rapid reloading of the gun. One of an interrupted-screw or sliding-block system sealed the breech to conserve firing velocity. One of the most succesful quick-firing designs was the Aquileian 'Canon de 75 modele 897.' This 75mm piece could fire fifteen rounds per minute of high_explosive and shrapnel, devastating attacking infantry. Other nations quickly copied the technology.
